analysis.one_liner: Overrides state laws that require overtime pay for farmworkers before a 60-hour workweek.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 2025 and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it has received no further action, no markup, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal labor law so that no state can require farmers to pay overtime to agricultural workers before they reach 60 hours in a week. Federal law already generally exempts farmworkers from overtime rules, but states are currently free to add stronger protections on top. States that have chosen to require farmworker overtime sooner than 60 hours would lose that authority, and their farmworkers would lose the extra pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Farm owners and agricultural employers, especially in states that have enacted overtime rules stricter than 60 hours. It would let them avoid the payroll cost of state-mandated overtime for long weeks during harvest, planting, and milking seasons.

how_it_helps.text: Amends Section 18 of the Fair Labor Standards Act so that federal law preempts any state law setting a maximum workweek for agricultural employees below 60 hours.

Under current federal law, agricultural employees are generally exempt from overtime requirements, so the practical effect of preemption is to erase stricter state overtime rules rather than replace them with a federal one.
Federal overtime rules today do not preempt state laws that give workers more protection; the bill removes that ability for states in this one area.
For farm employers in states with earlier overtime thresholds, the bill would eliminate the payroll cost of state-required overtime for weeks between 40 and 60 hours.

analysis.who_pays: Farmworkers in states that require overtime before 60 hours would lose that overtime pay. State governments would lose the authority they exercised to set their own labor standards, and the loss would fall hardest on the workers themselves.
analysis.who_pays_short: Farmworkers in states with overtime laws

drawbacks.text: The bill would void state overtime protections for agricultural workers in any state that set a threshold below 60 hours, meaning many farmworkers doing long weeks would no longer earn time-and-a-half under state law.
It takes away state governments' authority to set labor standards for workers within their borders, overriding rules those states enacted through their own democratic processes.
Even supporters would acknowledge the cost: it shifts a real expense, state-mandated overtime pay, away from farm employers and onto the workers who currently receive it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go entirely to farm employers as avoided labor costs, while the losses fall entirely on farmworkers who would surrender overtime pay they currently have under state law. There is no compensating benefit for workers in the bill; it does not create a federal overtime right to replace the state ones it preempts, since agricultural workers are already exempt from federal overtime.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on January 7, 2025 and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which has taken no further action on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 7, 2025 by Rep. Claudia Tenney with Reps. Langworthy and LaMalfa.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce the same day.
The complete action history shows no markup, no vote, and no further action after the referral.
It has 3 cosponsors, all Republicans, in addition to the sponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farmworkers in states with overtime protections are better off so far, because the bill has not advanced and those state rules remain in force. Farm employers avoid nothing yet either; the bill simply sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farmworkers, because the bill stalled in committee

for.name: Reps. Nick Langworthy and Doug LaMalfa
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and the cosponsors are Republicans, but no vote has occurred and no opposition has been recorded, so the partisan shape is not yet established.

industries.note: The bill would spare them the overtime pay that states like California and New York require for farm workweeks shorter than 60 hours, cutting their payroll costs. The savings come directly out of farmworkers' wages, so the industry's gain is the workers' loss.

Farmworkers in states with earlier overtime thresholds would lose time-and-a-half pay for long weeks. Farm work is seasonal and hours are often longest exactly when the bill would erase the overtime trigger.

analysis.trajectory: With only its three original sponsors, no additional cosponsors since January 2025, and no committee action, this bill follows the typical path of a member's ideological bill: it is likely to sit in the Education and Workforce Committee and expire at the end of the 119th Congress without ever receiving a vote.
